STEP 1 - Scene: A single whole apple (red and yellow-green, stem end facing up) resting on a white square plate. This is a snack, not a full meal.

STEP 2 - Vessel: White square plate, roughly 22 cm across (between a side plate and a dinner plate). Area ≈ 380 cm^2 (treating it as a 22 cm square-ish plate, approximately 3.14 x 11^2 ≈ 380 cm^2). The cable and wooden/metal frame at the edges are not food.

STEP 3 - Items: One whole apple.

STEP 4 - Area: The apple covers a circle about 8 cm across, roughly 50 cm^2, which is about 13% of the plate area. Food covers about 13% of the vessel total.

STEP 5 - Volume: An apple is roughly spherical, so its envelope is about 8 cm across and about 7.5 cm tall. Using footprint 50 cm^2 x 7.5 cm height gives about 375 ml gross volume. Apples are dense and fill most of their envelope, so a whole fruit is treated as a solid item.

STEP 6 - Grams: A medium apple weighs about 150-180 g. Using the fruit density from the guidance (0.5-0.7 g/ml) on a 375 ml envelope would give about 200-260 g, which is close to a typical medium apple. I take about 170 g as the best estimate for this apple, since its shape is round and it fills its envelope well.

STEP 7 - Energy: Raw apple is about 52 kcal per 100 g. 170 g x 0.52 = about 88 kcal.

STEP 8 - Sanity check: One medium apple at about 170 g and about 90 kcal is plausible for a single visible apple. It is far smaller than a full dinner plate, which matches the sparse coverage.
